data.content_ref: inline:The target's own mechanism text betrays a smuggled inductive commitment that contradicts its central claim. The claim explicitly requires 'the renunciation of any claim that the theory is probably true or reliable for long-term prediction,' and the mechanism insists corroboration 'implies no future probability.' Yet the very next sentence in the mechanism states that by choosing the most severely tested theory, scientists 'maximize the chance of quickly falsifying a false theory.' The phrase 'maximize the chance of quickly falsifying a false theory' is a forward-looking probabilistic assertion: it claims that a specific theory-selection rule will produce a specific future outcome (rapid falsification) at a higher rate than alternatives. If corroboration genuinely implies nothing about future performance, then there is no basis—no odds, no probability—for asserting that any selection rule 'maximizes the chance' of any future event. The target cannot simultaneously renounce all probabilistic predictions about the future and then ground its entire defense on 'maximizing the chance' of a future outcome. This is not an external philosophical objection but an internal contradiction within the target's own mechanism paragraph.
